Use this page when you are deciding whether a self-controlled or sibling
design fits your question, instead of a [comparison
cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) or matched [controls](case-control.qmd). Those
designs find a group to compare against and then adjust for confounding. The
designs here let the person themselves, or the family, be the control, so
confounding by what does not change over time (genes, fixed socioeconomic status
(SES), unmeasured lifestyle) is removed without you having to measure it. The
page tells you when each design applies and what it assumes; it has no worked
code, and the packages that do the work are linked in each section.

## Self-controlled designs (SCCS and case-crossover)

**Idea.** The person is their own control: you look at whether the outcome
happens more often in a short period right after a transient exposure than
in the person's other time. Because it is the same person, all confounding
that does not change over time (genes, sex, fixed SES, unmeasured lifestyle)
disappears, without you measuring it.

**When.** Transient exposure and acute outcome. Classic: a drug or vaccine and
an acute adverse event. SCCS was developed for vaccine safety ([Farrington
1995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7766778/)); the case-crossover design was
introduced for transient triggers of acute events such as myocardial infarction
([Maclure 1991](https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a115853)).

**Two variants:**

- **SCCS (self-controlled case series):** models the rate of the outcome
  within each person's follow-up and compares exposed vs. unexposed periods.
- **Case-crossover:** compares the exposure in a "hazard window" just before the
  event with the exposure in earlier reference windows in the same person.

**Assumptions** (otherwise the estimate is biased):

- the exposure is transient (not permanent);
- the event does not affect the probability of future exposure (and
  preferably not the length of follow-up either, e.g. if the outcome is death);
- the outcome is acute and well-defined in time.

**R.** The `SCCS` package (linked below) for self-controlled case series;
case-crossover can be done as conditional logistic regression
(`survival::clogit` with a `strata()` per person, see
[Regression](regression.qmd)).

## Sibling designs {#sibling-designs}

**Idea.** Compare siblings (or twins) within the same family. That holds
what siblings share, such as genes and upbringing environment, constant, and
you isolate the effect of what differs between them. Families are linked via the
parents' personal numbers in BEF ([DST, Nyt fra
Forskningsservice 4/2019](https://dst.dk/ext/2940168985/0/forskning/Ekstra-Nyt-fra-Forskningsservice-4-kvartal-2019--pdf)).
How to build the links, and which birth cohorts they cover, is on [Family
links](family-links.qmd).

**Analysis.** Conditional logistic regression or stratified Cox on the family
ID: the same strata idea as matched [case-control](case-control.qmd), just
with the family as the matched set.

**R.** `survival::clogit()` with a `strata()` per family, or `coxph()`
stratified by family ID (see [Regression](regression.qmd)). Packages for
pedigrees and sibling pairs (`kinship2`, `famnet`) are in [Algorithms and
packages](packages-overview.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
**A sibling design only removes shared confounding.** Non-shared confounding,
what differs between siblings (e.g. different birth weight or differences in
upbringing over time), remains. And if the exposure is strongly correlated
between siblings, the design can even amplify bias from remaining measurement
error. Use it deliberately, and report both the ordinary
and the sibling-controlled analysis.
:::

  an introduction to SCCS.
- [The `SCCS` package](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=SCCS) -

- Frisell, "[Invited Commentary: Sibling-Comparison Designs, Are They Worth the

:::
